statement: A teacher's rule is: "Every pupil who scores more than 40 points gets a star." The rule is always followed. Mo got a star. Lin did not get a star. Which of these must be true?

choices.misconception: I forgot that exactly 40 points is not more than 40, so Lin could have scored exactly 40.
I turned the rule round: it says a high score earns a star, not that a star needs a high score, so Mo may have got a star for another reason.
I thought Mo must have got the star for some other reason, but the rule allows Mo to have scored more than 40 as well.

choices.text: Nothing can be said about either pupil.
choices.misconception: I thought the rule only talks about pupils who scored more than 40, but it also tells us that Lin cannot have scored more than 40.

hints: Who does the rule force to get a star?
The rule says what must happen to high scorers. It says nothing about other reasons for getting a star. Ask: if Lin had scored more than 40, what would have happened?
If Lin had scored more than 40, Lin would have a star. But Lin has no star.

solutions.reliable: If Lin had scored more than 40, the rule would have given Lin a star. Lin has no star, so Lin did not score more than 40: Lin scored 40 points or fewer. For Mo, the rule never says that only high scorers get stars, so Mo could have scored anything. The transferable idea: from "if A then B" and "not B" you may conclude "not A", but from B alone you cannot conclude A.

whyOnTest: Precise reading of an if-then rule is tested: the rule works backwards from a missing star, but not from a star that is there.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
